events.promise: Resend’s documented test addresses let the engineer inspect three important event paths with non-production recipients before deciding whether to route real transactional messages through Resend.
events.arc: Move directly from the available test mechanism to one bounded evaluation: read the documentation, run the same harmless payload against the three documented outcomes, and inspect what Resend exposes.

emails.job: Get the engineer to review and, if appropriate, run the documented three-outcome test before routing real transactional messages through Resend.
emails.single_idea: Vary only the test recipient to simulate delivered, bounced, and spam-complaint outcomes, then inspect how each result appears before connecting real recipients.
emails.objection: A simulated event is useful for checking instrumentation and handler paths, but it cannot establish how production messages will perform with real mailbox providers.
must_not_say: Do not claim that this test proves production deliverability, inbox placement, throughput, or reliability.
Do not assume the reader uses a particular provider, auth platform, framework, SDK, or SMTP setup.
Do not imply that the reader has experienced a bounce, complaint, outage, rate-limit error, or prior incident.
Do not frame this as a full migration, production-readiness test, or provider comparison.
Do not claim that test sends are free or excluded from quota; they count against the account quota.
Do not imply that application webhook events appear without a publicly accessible endpoint and a webhook configured in Resend.
Do not introduce pricing, plan limits, dedicated IPs, customer testimonials, marketing email, templates, automations, or security claims.
emails.felt_need: Auth email sending (signup confirmation, OTP, magic link, invites) gets blocked with a 429 email rate limit error under normal usage, even when the reporter believes they are under the documented limit.
emails.status_quo: Checks the platform's own Auth logs in the dashboard to verify whether the documented email limit was actually exceeded.
emails.mechanism: Make the documentation the first step. It provides Resend’s delivered, bounced, and spam-complaint test addresses. Send the same harmless test payload to each address one at a time, then compare the resulting events in the Emails Dashboard; if a webhook endpoint is already configured, also confirm that each JSON event reaches the intended handler. Receiving events in an application requires a public endpoint and a webhook configured in Resend.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Resend’s documented test workflow exposes enough information to evaluate the three event paths before configuring real recipient traffic.
emails.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Resend supplies test recipient addresses for delivered, bounced, and spam-complaint events without affecting domain reputation.
emails.next_step_limit: Reading the documentation does not execute the test, validate an application webhook endpoint, or establish production deliverability.

events.body:
With Resend, you can inspect delivered, bounced, and spam-complaint event paths before sending to real recipients. Resend is a transactional email platform that exposes sending outcomes in its Dashboard, API, and webhooks.

Send the same harmless payload, one address at a time, to delivered@resend.dev, bounced@resend.dev, and complained@resend.dev. Then compare the resulting events in the Emails Dashboard.

If you have a public endpoint and a webhook configured in Resend, confirm that each JSON event reaches the intended handler. This checks instrumentation and handler paths; it does not establish production deliverability.

Review the test-address documentation, then decide whether to run the three-outcome check.

This test checks event instrumentation and handler behavior without affecting domain reputation. It does not establish production deliverability with real mailbox providers.

readers.persona:
Selected audience (explicit constraints): The one backend engineer at a ten-person product team who owns email because nobody else does.
The context and problem reports below describe observed members of this market, not established experiences or installed tools of this recipient. The campaign request controls which job this email addresses; do not require a link to an unrequested integration in your doubts or click requirements.
Observed context (grounded; applicability must be checked): Individual engineers integrating a hosted auth platform (Supabase Auth) into a product's signup, password-reset, invite, and OTP flows post first-person accounts, in GitHub issues and discussions on the platform's own repos, of hitting the built-in email rate limit and having to reason through Supabase's dashboard logs, SMTP settings, and plan tiers themselves to diagnose it.
Source: https://github.com/supabase/supabase/issues/34209; quote: I am experiencing an issue where authentication emails (magic links/OTP) are blocked with a 429: email rate limit exceeded error, even though I have not exceeded the email limits.
Source: https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/35315; quote: I'm encountering a persistent 429 (Too Many Requests) error with the message AuthApiError: email rate limit exceeded when calling supabase.auth.signUp from my React frontend application.
Problem context: Auth email sending (signup confirmation, OTP, magic link, invites) gets blocked with a 429 email rate limit error under normal usage, even when the reporter believes they are under the documented limit.; source: https://github.com/supabase/supabase/issues/34209
Problem context: Upgrading the platform's paid subscription tier does not raise the built-in email rate limit; only configuring a separate custom SMTP provider does.; source: https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/35286
Problem context: An unrelated dashboard action (creating or deleting an Auth Hook) silently wipes the custom SMTP configuration and resets the email rate limit back to a low default, with no warning shown in the UI, and the effect on real auth email only becomes visible later.; source: https://github.com/supabase/supabase/issues/49873
Problem context: It is unclear to the reporter how the platform counts emails and API calls toward its documented rate limit, since the observed failure point does not match the documented threshold.; source: https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/29167
Problem context: Mixing transactional and marketing email sending on the same provider/domain creates a deliverability risk: a marketing-driven spam complaint or unsubscribe spike can get the account suspended and take down transactional (auth-critical) sending with it.; source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41594209
Problem context: A homegrown transactional-email setup (enums, templates, tracking) that starts simple for signup/password-reset grows into an unwieldy system as a SaaS product and its users grow, without anyone wanting to fully outsource it.; source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21486289
readers.what_it_sells: Resend is a transactional email platform offering test addresses so I can verify delivery, bounce, complaint, dashboard, and optional webhook events before sending real email.
readers.biggest_doubt: I am not given a reason to evaluate Resend today or enough context to know whether this workflow applies to our current email setup.
fixes: Rewrite "Before routing transactional email to real recipients, you can inspect how three outcomes appear in Resend." to acknowledge the missing context: "If you're evaluating Resend for transactional email, you can test its delivered, bounced, and complaint events before changing production routing."
Rewrite "See addresses and inspection workflow" to state the effort and prerequisites, for example: "View the 2-minute test workflow and required setup."
Cut the duplicated CTA text: "See addresses and inspection workflow" appears twice.
